title: CircuitPython data types
text:
Core built-in data types
In CircuitPython, data types are mostly the same as Python, but with important constraints due to limited memory and performance on microcontrollers.
Below is a complete, practical overview of CircuitPython data types, with notes on when and why to use each.

title: CircuitPython data types
text:
NoneType
x = None


Represents “no value”
Common for defaults or placeholders



Boolean (bool)
True, False

Used for logic and conditions
Very small memory footprint



Integers (int)
x = 42

Arbitrary precision in theory
In practice: limited by available RAM
Much cheaper than floats

📌 Use ints whenever possible


Floating Point (float)
x = 3.14

32-bit floats (single precision)
Slower and more memory-hungry
Avoid in tight loops if possible

title: CircuitPython data types
text:
Text & Binary Data

Strings (str)
s = "hello"

UTF-8 strings
Immutable (cannot be changed in place)
Repeated concatenation causes fragmentation

📌 Prefer building strings carefully or using buffers


Bytes (bytes)
b = b"ABC"

Immutable sequence of bytes
Efficient for binary data
Common in I/O and communication



Bytearray (bytearray)
buf = bytearray(10)

Mutable sequence of bytes
Very memory-efficient
Excellent for buffers, sensors, displays

⭐ Highly recommended for performance

title: CircuitPython data types
text:
Collections

Tuple (tuple)
t = (1, 2, 3)

Immutable
Lower overhead than lists
Good for constants



List (list)
lst = [1, 2, 3]

Mutable
Higher memory overhead
Avoid large or frequently resized lists



Dictionary (dict)
d = {"a": 1, "b": 2}

High memory cost
Slower than lists/tuples
Use sparingly on microcontrollers



Set (set)
s = {1, 2, 3}

Supported, but expensive in memory
Rarely used in CircuitPython projects

title: CircuitPython data types
text:
Special & Advanced Types

Range (range)
for i in range(10):

Memory-efficient
Does not create a list
Always prefer over list(range())



Memoryview (memoryview)
mv = memoryview(buf)

Zero-copy view of buffers
Extremely efficient
Ideal for slicing bytearrays

⭐ Advanced but very powerful


Function (function)
def foo():
    pass

First-class objects
Minimal overhead



Class / Object (object)
class Foo:
    pass

Supported
Each instance uses memory
Avoid heavy OOP patterns

title: CircuitPython data types
text:
Not Available or Limited



Type
Status




complex
❌ Not supported


decimal
❌ Not supported


fractions
❌ Not supported


numpy
❌ Not available


Large recursion
⚠️ Limited stack

title: CircuitPython data types
text:
Performance & Memory Guidance (Very Important)
Best choices for microcontrollers
✔ int
✔ bool
✔ tuple
✔ range
✔ bytearray
✔ memoryview
Use sparingly
⚠️ float
⚠️ list
⚠️ dict
⚠️ set
⚠️ str concatenation
In summary, CircuitPython supports most core Python data types, but memory-efficient types like int, bytearray, and range are strongly preferred.

title: Testing your board
text:
Flash onboard LED
https://github.com/WaylandM/Biomaker-CircuitPython/blob/main/examples/flash_onboard_led/code.py
Content of code.py:
import time
import board
import digitalio

led = digitalio.DigitalInOut(board.LED)
led.direction = digitalio.Direction.OUTPUT

while True:
    led.value = True   # LED on
    time.sleep(0.5)
    led.value = False  # LED off
    time.sleep(0.5)
This script will:

Set up the onboard LED pin as a digital output.
Turn in on for 0.5 seconds.
Turn it off for 0.5 seconds.
Repeat this on-off cycle indefinitely.

Let’s go through the example line by line and explain what each part does.
import time
import board
import digitalio

time gives access to timing functions like sleep().
board contains names for the physical pins on your specific board (like board.LED).
digitalio lets you control pins as simple on/off digital signals.

led = digitalio.DigitalInOut(board.LED)

board.LED is a predefined pin that’s connected to the onboard LED.
DigitalInOut(...) creates an object that lets you control that pin.
The variable led now represents the LED pin.

led.direction = digitalio.Direction.OUTPUT

Pins can be inputs (read signals) or outputs (send signals).
Here we set the LED pin to be an output, so we can drive it on and off.

while True:

This starts an infinite loop.
Everything indented underneath will repeat forever until the board is reset or powered off.

    led.value = True   # LED on

Setting value to True sends a HIGH signal to the pin.
On most boards this turns the LED on.

    time.sleep(0.5)

Pause the program for 0.5 seconds (500 milliseconds).
The LED stays on during this pause.

    led.value = False  # LED off

Setting value to False sends a LOW signal.
This turns the LED off.

    time.sleep(0.5)

Wait another 0.5 seconds with the LED off.
Then the loop repeats, so the LED turns on again.

Overall behaviour:

Turn LED on
Wait half a second
Turn LED off
Wait half a second
Repeat forever

That creates a steady blink: on–off–on–off every second.

title: Testing your board
text:
Flash onboard NeoPixel
https://github.com/WaylandM/Biomaker-CircuitPython/tree/main/examples/flash_onboard_neopixel_led
Content of code.py:
import time
import board
import neopixel

pixel = neopixel.NeoPixel(board.NEOPIXEL, 1)

while True:
    pixel[0] = (50, 0, 0)  # red
    time.sleep(0.5)
    pixel[0] = (0, 0, 0)   # off
    time.sleep(0.5)
Line by line explanation:
pixel = neopixel.NeoPixel(board.NEOPIXEL, 1)

Creates a NeoPixel controller on the pin connected to the onboard RGB LED.
1 means there is one pixel.

pixel[0] = (50, 0, 0)

Sets pixel 0 to a colour using RGB values.
(50, 0, 0) = red (brightness 50 out of 255).

pixel[0] = (0, 0, 0)

Sets the pixel to black (all channels 0) = off.

The same infinite loop and time.sleep(0.5) calls make it blink on and off.
In both cases, you’re just repeatedly:

writing a value to the LED
waiting a bit
writing the opposite value
waiting again

title: Testing your Arduino Sensor Kit Base
text:
Non-blocking LED blink
A non-blocking blink means the LED toggles based on time checks instead of time.sleep(). This lets the microcontroller do other work in the loop (read sensors, handle buttons, etc.) while the LED blinks.
import time
import board
import digitalio

led = digitalio.DigitalInOut(board.GP4)
led.direction = digitalio.Direction.OUTPUT

blink_interval = 0.5  # seconds
last_toggle = time.monotonic()

while True:
    current_time = time.monotonic()

    if current_time - last_toggle >= blink_interval:
        led.value = not led.value
        last_toggle = current_time

    # Other code can run here without being blocked
    # Example:
    # read sensors
    # check buttons

Why this is better
time.sleep() blocks the CPU. Using time.monotonic():

loop keeps running continuously
multiple tasks can run at once
timing stays consistent

title: Testing your Arduino Sensor Kit Base
text:
PWM LED Fade (Smooth Breathing Effect)
To fade an LED with PWM in CircuitPython, you use the pwmio module and gradually change the duty cycle.

import time
import board
import pwmio

# Create PWM output on LED pin
led = pwmio.PWMOut(board.GP4, frequency=1000)

while True:
    # Fade in
    for duty in range(0, 65535, 500):
        led.duty_cycle = duty
        time.sleep(0.01)

    # Fade out
    for duty in range(65535, 0, -500):
        led.duty_cycle = duty
        time.sleep(0.01)

How it works

duty_cycle range: 0 → 65535
0 = LED off
65535 = full brightness
Increasing the duty cycle gradually creates the fade-in effect.

title: Testing your Arduino Sensor Kit Base
text:
Optional: breathing LED (continuous smooth loop)
import time
import board
import pwmio

led = pwmio.PWMOut(board.GP4, frequency=1000)

brightness = 0
fade_amount = 500

while True:
    led.duty_cycle = brightness
    brightness += fade_amount

    if brightness <= 0 or brightness >= 65535:
        fade_amount = -fade_amount

    time.sleep(0.01)
This produces a continuous breathing effect often used as a status indicator.

title: Testing your Arduino Sensor Kit Base
text:
Gamma-Corrected LED Fade
Gamma correction makes LED fading look smooth to human eyes. Without it, most brightness change appears at the high end because human vision is non-linear. Gamma correction compensates for that.
Typical gamma value: ~2.2
import time
import board
import pwmio
import math

led = pwmio.PWMOut(board.GP4, frequency=1000)

gamma = 2.2
steps = 100

while True:
    # Fade in
    for i in range(steps):
        x = i / (steps - 1)
        corrected = math.pow(x, gamma)
        led.duty_cycle = int(corrected * 65535)
        time.sleep(0.01)

    # Fade out
    for i in reversed(range(steps)):
        x = i / (steps - 1)
        corrected = math.pow(x, gamma)
        led.duty_cycle = int(corrected * 65535)
        time.sleep(0.01)

Key idea
Brightness is corrected like this:
corrected = brightness ^ gamma
Example (gamma ≈ 2.2):



Linear input
Perceived brightness
PWM output




0.1
very dim
~0.006


0.5
medium
~0.22


0.8
bright
~0.61



This produces a much smoother fade, especially at low brightness.

title: Testing your Arduino Sensor Kit Base
text:
Faster Method (Gamma Lookup Table)
Computing pow() every loop is slower on microcontrollers. A lookup table is faster.
import time
import board
import pwmio

led = pwmio.PWMOut(board.GP4, frequency=1000)

gamma = 2.2
steps = 100

# Precompute gamma table
gamma_table = [
    int((i / (steps - 1)) ** gamma * 65535)
    for i in range(steps)
]

while True:
    for v in gamma_table:
        led.duty_cycle = v
        time.sleep(0.01)

    for v in reversed(gamma_table):
        led.duty_cycle = v
        time.sleep(0.01)
Benefits:

smoother animation
less CPU work
better for multiple LEDs

title: Testing your Arduino Sensor Kit Base
text:
Bonus: Perceptually Smooth Breathing LED
import time
import board
import pwmio
import math

led = pwmio.PWMOut(board.GP4, frequency=1000)

t = 0

while True:
    brightness = (math.sin(t) + 1) / 2
    corrected = brightness ** 2.2
    led.duty_cycle = int(corrected * 65535)

    t += 0.05
    time.sleep(0.01)
This produces a very smooth Apple-style breathing LED.
